title: Why Most Agent Demos Never Survive Contact With Production
linkedin_md:
# Why Most Agent Demos Never Survive Contact With Production

Most agent demos work because the environment is kind.

The task is narrow. The inputs are clean. The tools respond quickly. The user is patient. The model gets one happy path, maybe two, and the demo ends before reality has time to show up.

Production is different.

In production, users paste malformed data. APIs timeout. Permissions are missing. Tool schemas drift. One call succeeds and the next one fails. The model gets distracted by irrelevant context. The same workflow that looked magical in a 90-second demo now needs retries, audit logs, cost controls, latency budgets, and a way to explain what happened when the output is wrong.

That is where most agents break.

Not because the model is useless. Not because tool use is fake. But because the demo tested capability, while production tests reliability.

[YOUR STORY HERE - 2-3 paragraphs]

## The Demo Optimizes For Impressiveness

A good demo answers the question: can this agent do the task at all?

That is a useful question. It is just not the final one.

A production system has to answer different questions:

Can it do the task 10,000 times?

Can it recover when step 4 fails?

Can it avoid taking irreversible action without confirmation?

Can it stay inside budget?

Can it produce the same class of result tomorrow after the model changes?

Can an engineer debug it at 2 a.m. without replaying a full conversation by hand?

Most demos skip those questions because they make the system look less magical. In production, those questions are the product.

## Agents Fail At The Boundaries

The agent loop is rarely the hardest part.

The hard parts are the boundaries around the loop.

Inputs need validation. Tools need strict contracts. Intermediate state needs to be stored somewhere inspectable. Outputs need verification. Risky actions need gating. Failures need to be classified. The system needs to know the difference between "try again", "ask the user", "escalate", and "stop".

A demo can let the model improvise across these boundaries.

A production system cannot.

If your agent can send emails, update records, issue refunds, modify code, or trigger jobs, then every tool call is part of your application surface area. Treating those calls as casual model side effects is how you get silent data corruption with a friendly chat transcript on top.

## Autonomy Has A Budget

Autonomy sounds binary. Either the agent acts on its own or it does not.

In practice, autonomy is a budget.

You give the system some number of steps, some amount of money, some time window, some permission scope, and some failure tolerance. When it exceeds those limits, it stops or asks.

A production agent should have clear limits like:

Maximum tool calls per run: 10, 25, 50, depending on the task.

Maximum wall-clock time: maybe 30 seconds for interactive work, several minutes for background jobs.

Maximum spend: per user, per task, per day.

Maximum irreversible actions: usually zero without explicit confirmation.

Maximum uncertainty: if confidence is low, route to a human or ask a targeted question.

Without budgets, "agentic" often becomes "unbounded loop with vibes".

## The Tool Layer Matters More Than The Prompt

Prompts are important, but they are not load-bearing enough on their own.

The tool layer should make bad behavior difficult.

Use narrow tools instead of giant generic ones. Prefer `create_invoice_draft` over `execute_sql`. Prefer typed arguments over free-form blobs. Add server-side validation. Return structured errors. Make actions idempotent. Include dry-run modes for anything risky.

The model should not have to remember every invariant. The system should enforce them.

If a tool can only accept valid account IDs, valid date ranges, and authorized operations, you have removed entire classes of failure before the model gets involved.

Good agent engineering looks less like writing a perfect prompt and more like designing a boring, well-fenced distributed system.

## Observability Is Not Optional

If you cannot inspect the agent's behavior, you do not have a production system.

You need traces for model calls, tool calls, arguments, return values, retries, failure types, latency, token usage, and final outcomes. You need to know where time is going. You need to know which tools fail most often. You need to know whether the agent is asking too many questions, taking too many steps, or silently producing low-quality work.

A useful trace answers:

What did the model see?

What did it decide?

Which tool did it call?

What came back?

Why did it continue, stop, or ask the user?

What changed in the outside world?

Without this, debugging becomes folklore. Someone reads a transcript, guesses what happened, edits the prompt, and hopes.

That does not scale.

## Evaluation Has To Include The Mess

Many agent evals are too clean.

They test the golden path. They check whether the final answer looks right. They ignore latency, retries, tool failures, partial completion, permission errors, ambiguous user intent, stale context, and malformed inputs.

Production evals should include the mess.

Build test cases where the first tool call fails. Where the user asks for something impossible. Where two records have similar names. Where the model has enough information to proceed, but only if it chooses the safer path. Where the correct behavior is to refuse, ask a question, or stop.

For agents, success is not always completing the task.

Sometimes success is not doing the wrong thing.

[YOUR STORY HERE - 2-3 paragraphs]

## The Real Takeaways

Most agent demos die because they confuse intelligence with reliability.

A model that can reason through a task once is useful. A system that can execute that task repeatedly, safely, cheaply, and observably is production software.

If you are building agents for real users, focus on the unglamorous parts:

Define the task boundary.

Constrain the tools.

Set budgets.

Persist state.

Classify failures.

Add human review where actions are costly.

Trace every step.

Evaluate against messy cases.

Make the system stop cleanly.

The better your production agent gets, the less it looks like a magic trick. It starts to look like a normal service with a model inside it.

That is the point.

The model brings flexibility. The engineering brings survival.
